# 1.1 Introduction

## What You'll Learn in this Chapter (and the Four Big Steps)

Welcome! In this chapter you'll learn many things.

You'll learn about recognizing arguments. In particular, you'll learn

-   what arguments are, and
-   how to recognize arguments by spotting expressions, like "therefore"
    and "because."

You'll learn about analyzing arguments. In particular, you'll learn

-   how to identify the important claims in an argument, ignoring
    questions and commands,
-   how to recognize one important way that claims can be connected to
    each other, and
-   how to map arguments composed of one premise and an ultimate
    conclusion. (What are premises and ultimate conclusions and what
    does it mean to "map" an argument? We'll get to that.)

You'll learn about evaluating arguments and communicating your
evaluation of an argument. In particular, you'll learn

-   how to evaluate premises (We'll see what premises are in a bit.),
-   how to evaluate inferences (We'll see what inferences are in a bit,
    too.),
-   how to evaluate an argument composed of one premise and an ultimate
    conclusion once you've evaluated the premise and the inference in
    the argument,
-   how your evaluation of an argument should affect your belief in the
    ultimate conclusion, and
-   how to express your evaluation of an argument.

You'll learn about constructing arguments and communicating arguments.
In particular, you'll learn

-   how to construct arguments composed of one premise and an ultimate
    conclusion, and
-   how to write passages containing arguments composed of one premise
    and an ultimate conclusion.

We can think of **recognizing**, **analyzing**, **evaluating**, and
**constructing** arguments as the ***Four Big Steps*** of critical
thinking. We'll be applying them over and over again to a series of
passages throughout this textbook.

## How to Read this Text

As you can see, you'll be getting a lot of information here. You'll be
getting a lot of information in other chapters, too, and it can be easy
to feel overwhelmed and intimidated. But don't worry! Learning how to
recognize, analyze, evaluate, and construct arguments is easier than
learning how to read and write, and you've already done that! Keep an
open mind and a light heart and this will be fun.

Here are some tips that have helped other people to learn from this
text:

### 1. Focus on *Understanding*, not *Remembering*, what you Read.

The chapters will introduce concepts and skills by walking you through a
series of examples. As you read each example in the text, focus on
***understanding*** what we're saying, but don't worry about
***remembering*** all of it. Why? Because if you understand it,
eventually you *will* remember it, but if you *just* remember it, you
may never understand it. Besides, we'll keep track of the important
points of each example for you by summarizing these points at the end of
each example. At the end of each chapter, we'll provide you with a
handbook that summarizes the important points of the chapter as a whole.
You can always return to the example summaries and chapter handbooks to
remind yourself of the concepts and skills you're learning.

### 2. Reflect upon the Summaries.

Pay special attention to the summaries provided after each example.
These summaries review the main points of the examples. If something in
a summary doesn't make sense, review the example again until things
start to come into focus.

### 3. End with the Handbook.

As we noted, each of the chapters comes with a handbook that summarizes
all of the most important concepts and skills in the textbook up to that
point.

When you've finished a chapter, review the handbook because it
represents a comprehensive summary of what you've learned so far. And
it's called a "handbook" for a reason: it's intended to be something
that you can take with you and use as you encounter and construct
arguments in a variety of contexts. In a sense, the purpose of this
textbook is to teach you how to use the (continually evolving) handbook,
and the purpose of the final handbook is to help you apply what you've
learned after the course is over. Eventually, of course, you'll
internalize the handbook and you won't need it anymore, but you can use
it for as long as you like - for months or for years after you finish
this book.

If you follow those tips, we're confident that you'll find learning this
material to be manageable and fun! So let's get to it. We'll start by
defining some important concepts and terms.

## Arguments: Claims and Connections

In everyday life, the word "**argument**" often refers to a fight. We
aren't going to use the word that way. Instead, for our purposes, an
argument will be any attempt to convince someone of something by setting
out reasons to back it up. Our technical definition will be:

> An argument is a unit of reasoning that attempts to establish that one
> claim is true by citing other claims as evidence.

Suppose, for example, that someone says the following:

> "Sunshine Soda is nutritious. Therefore Sunshine Soda should be
> included in school lunches."

This is an argument because it's trying to convince us of something.
Specifically, this argument is trying to convince us that Sunshine Soda
should be included in school lunches. The claim that the argument tries
to establish as true (e.g., "Sunshine Soda should be included in school
lunches") is called the "**ultimate conclusion**" and sometimes it's
just called "the conclusion."

> "Sunshine Soda is nutritious. Therefore Sunshine Soda should be
> included in school lunches."

-   This passage contains an argument.
-   "Sunshine Soda should be included in school lunches" is the ultimate
    conclusion.

Other claims in an argument are offered in support of the ultimate
conclusion, but the ultimate conclusion itself is not offered in support
of any other claim. The ultimate conclusion is where the argument stops.
(That's why it's called "ultimate.") Every argument has exactly one
ultimate conclusion.

Now, what about the sentence, "Sunshine Soda is nutritious"? That's
being used as evidence to convince us that Sunshine Soda should be
included in school lunches, but the argument doesn't give us any reason
to believe it. Instead, the argument simply states that Sunshine Soda is
nutritious and expects us to accept it.

Claims that the argument uses as evidence for the ultimate conclusion,
but that the argument assumes to be true without providing evidence for
them, are called "**premises**." Every argument has at least one premise
because every argument has to start somewhere.

> "Sunshine Soda is nutritious. Therefore Sunshine Soda should be
> included in school lunches."

-   This passage contains an argument.
-   "Sunshine Soda should be included in school lunches" is the ultimate
    conclusion.
-   "Sunshine Soda is nutritious" is a premise.

Ultimate conclusions and premises are claims in an argument --
assertions that are either true or false -- and we can usually point at
claims, or at least state them. But arguments are made up of *more* than
claims. **Arguments are made up of claims and connections between the
claims**. (That's important.) And the connections between the claims can
be the hardest part to see.

In the argument we're considering, the connection between "Sunshine Soda
is nutritious" and "Sunshine Soda should be included in school lunches,"
is the connection that says, essentially, *"You should take the fact
that Sunshine Soda is nutritious as a reason to accept that it should be
included in school lunches."*

The relationship that says, *"You should take this claim as a reason to
accept that other claim,"* is called an *inference*. Our technical
definition will be "an **inference** is the connection that holds
between a set of claims, call it 'R' for 'reason,' and another claim,
call it 'C' for 'conclusion,' when the truth of the claims in R is
supposed to establish the truth of claim C."

In our example argument, the inference was indicated with the word
"therefore."

> "Sunshine Soda is nutritious. Therefore Sunshine Soda should be
> included in school lunches."

-   This passage contains an argument.
-   "Sunshine Soda should be included in school lunches" is the ultimate
    conclusion.
-   "Sunshine Soda is nutritious" is a premise.
-   "Therefore" indicates the inference between the premise and the
    ultimate conclusion.

Sometimes, though, the inference won't have a special word to represent
it. If we remove the word "therefore" from our example, for instance,
the inference will still be there because the connection between the
premise and ultimate conclusion will still be there.

> "Sunshine Soda is nutritious. Sunshine Soda should be included in
> school lunches."

-   This passage contains an argument.
-   "Sunshine Soda should be included in school lunches" is the ultimate
    conclusion.
-   "Sunshine Soda is nutritious" is a premise.
-   The inference is the connection between the premise and the ultimate
    conclusion.

That's one of the reasons why inferences, and connections between claims
in general, can be harder to identify than the claims themselves: they
can be *invisible*. And, of course, that can pose a real problem.

Because arguments are composed of claims and connections, understanding
an argument involves understanding what 1) claims make up the argument
and 2) how those claims are connected to each other. *To the extent that
we don't understand (or even see) the connections, then, we don't
understand the argument*.

And why is it important to understand an argument? Because an argument
is trying to *convince* us of something, and we want to make sure that
we're being convinced when we should be convinced and that we aren't
being convinced when we shouldn't be convinced.

## Argument Maps to the Rescue!

Fortunately, there's a way to represent arguments that makes the claims
and the connections between the claims much easier to see and
understand. It's called "argument mapping."

Because an argument attempts to take us from premises to a conclusion,
we can think of an argument like a map that tries to show us how to get
from one point to another.

Let's say that the ultimate conclusion is a golden boulder that we're
trying to reach. It's our destination.

![](/images/ch01/golden_boulder.png){.illustration width=150px fig-alt="A golden boulder."}

Premises are the places on the map that we start from. They're boulders,
too.

![](/images/ch01/starting_boulder.png){.illustration width=140px fig-alt="A gray boulder."}

How do we get from one boulder to another? By crossing a bridge! The
bridges are inferences.

![](/images/ch01/ladder.png){.illustration width=80px fig-alt="A wooden ladder standing upright."}

Thinking about it this way, we can draw a map of the argument that we've
been considering. "Sunshine Soda should be included in the school
lunches" is the golden boulder that we're trying to reach. "Sunshine
Soda is nutritious," is the boulder we're starting from. And the
inference between them is a bridge connecting the two.

![](/images/ch01/boulders_soda_labeled.png){.illustration width=300px fig-alt="A ladder leads from a gray boulder up to a golden boulder. The gray boulder is labeled \"Sunshine Soda is nutritious.\" The ladder is labeled \"Inference.\" The golden boulder is labeled \"Sunshine Soda should be included in school lunches.\""}

This map clearly displays (and allows us to distinguish between) the two
different things that make up arguments: Boulders and Bridges -- or, in
the terminology we'll be using, Claims and Connections!

We won't usually be drawing boulders and bridges, of course. Instead,
our maps will look like this:

![The Sunshine Soda argument as an argument map.](/images/ch01/Soda.png){#fig-1-1-soda width=209px fig-alt="Argument map concluding: Sunshine Soda should be included in school lunches. A full text description is provided."}

::: {.map-outline fig="fig-1-1-soda"}
{{< include /outlines/ch01/Soda_list.md >}}
:::

The principle, however, is exactly the same. The boxes with claims are
like boulders; the vertical green connecting line is like a bridge; and
the map shows us how the argument tries to take us from the claim on the
bottom to the claim at the top.

### Applying the Four Big Steps of Critical Thinking (and Starting Small)

We're faced with arguments every day because people are often trying to
get us to believe things. Furthermore, we frequently want to convince
*other* people that something is true.

Consequently, it would be nice if we could:

1)  recognize *when* someone is trying to convince us of something,
2)  determine *how* this person is trying to convince us,
3)  figure out if the person is giving us *good* reasons for the
    position advanced, and
4)  *make* a convincing case for our own position

In short, we want to:

1)  *recognize* arguments,
2)  *analyze* arguments,
3)  *evaluate* arguments and *communicate* that evaluation to others,
    and
4)  *construct* arguments and *communicate* our arguments to others.

As we've seen, these are the Four Big Steps of critical thinking. We'll
be developing a procedure here, a sequence of steps that we can follow
in order to understand, evaluate and construct any argument we want, and
we'll be practicing this procedure a *lot* because procedures are best
learned through repetition. That way, they become internalized.

Of course, we'll be learning new things as we go along, and so we'll be
presented with new examples to help us understand and master those new
concepts and skills. All the examples in a chapter will have a common
theme (this chapter, for instance, will focus on advertisements) but the
critical thinking skills that you'll learn by working through these
examples apply to any content.

Arguments, and the passages containing them, can be *very* complex and
we'll be seeing some pretty complicated ones later. For now, we'll start
with short passages. By enabling us to focus on one thing at a time,
without being distracted by unnecessary complexity, these small
arguments will allow us to isolate and practice specific skills in order
to fully master them before progressing.

A quick word of advice: because these arguments are short, there is the
risk that you might find some of these examples fairly easy and be
tempted to rush through them. Please resist this temptation! **Thinking
about what you're doing *now*, with small arguments, will help you to
internalize the process, and this will make the complex arguments that
you'll face later on *much* easier to handle**.

It's a lot like learning to swim. You don't *need* to swim when you're
in four feet of water; if you don't want to swim, you can simply stand
up and walk to shore. Nevertheless, it's a good idea to *learn* *how* to
swim in four feet of water, and to get completely comfortable with the
strokes, *before* the only alternative to swimming is sinking.

It's time to look at our first example and work through each of the Four
Big Steps!
